identity.title: Compositional Generalization Requires Linear, Orthogonal Representations in Vision Embedding Models

problem.claim: The paper asks what representational structure supports generalization to unseen combinations of familiar concepts.

contributions.claim: Formalizes divisibility, transferability, and stability, and reports that under standard training these desiderata impose linear decomposition into per-concept components that are orthogonal across concepts.
Connects the Linear Representation Hypothesis to compositional generalization as a necessary consequence and derives dimension bounds relating composable-concept counts to embedding geometry.

Reports partial linear factorization with low-rank, near-orthogonal per-concept factors across CLIP, SigLIP, and DINO, with the structure's degree correlating with generalization to unseen combinations.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors present a necessary-geometric-constraints account of compositional generalization, including dimension bounds linking composable concepts to embedding geometry.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report partial linear factorization and low-rank, near-orthogonal per-concept factors in CLIP, SigLIP, and DINO.
The authors report that the degree of this structure correlates with compositional generalization on unseen combinations.

narrative_sequence.summary: Modern models encounter only a small fraction of the combinatorial input space, motivating compositional generalization.
The paper asks what representation structure is required for generalization to unseen concept combinations.
Three desiderata are formalized and reported to require linear per-concept decomposition with cross-concept orthogonality, yielding dimension bounds.
Across three vision embedding models, the authors report partial versions of this geometry and a correlation with unseen-combination generalization.
The conditions are presented as predictions about geometry to which increasingly scaled models may converge.

source_observation.claim: The abstract pairs formal desiderata and geometric constraints with measurable representation properties, then relates those properties to compositional generalization across named model families.

lessons.interpretation: This makes a structural theory legible by aligning its abstract conditions with observable diagnostics and an outcome measure.
lessons.application: Define each theoretical representation condition operationally, report its diagnostic separately, and test whether diagnostic strength tracks the target capability across model families.
lessons.exception: Avoid this framing when the proposed structure has no defensible observable proxy or the target outcome cannot be measured independently.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the formal definitions, proof assumptions, dimension-bound formulas, or what 'standard training' entails.
The reported correlations do not establish causation, and no effect sizes, statistical details, evaluation protocols, or comparison baselines are given.
The abstract does not clarify how partial factorization, low rank, near orthogonality, or convergence predictions are quantified.
